final_message:
Subject: The garden, the rain, and other disappointments

Dear Marcus,

You asked on Monday how the garden was coming on. I will tell you, though I do it with a heavy heart, and a heavier pair of boots, which are at this moment standing in the hall in a pool of their own making.

It has rained for nine days. I do not mean the pleasant rain that the poets are fond of, which falls softly on the roses and makes the birds sing; I mean a steady, businesslike, Presbyterian rain, that has no intention of stopping until it has seen the whole job through. The beds are under water. The peas, which I put in with great ceremony and some speeches, have gone to the bottom like a lot of small green Atlantic cables. The lettuce is floating. I looked out this morning and saw a row of what I took to be turnips, and what proved on inspection to be a family of ducks, who had come to look at the property and seemed to think well of it.

My plan, as you may remember, was to spend this weekend setting out the tomato plants. I had them all laid out in my mind: so many here, so many there, a stake for each, and a short moral lecture for the cutworms. Polly says that a man who plans a tomato-bed in October is either an optimist or a fool, and that in my case the two conditions are not easily told apart. But she is wrong about the date; I am only a little behind, and the almanac, which I consult chiefly when it agrees with me, says the frost is late this year.

The worst of it is the sense of injury. When you have made up your mind to hoe, and have put on the old hat, and have got the hoe down from the nail, and then the heavens open, you feel that Nature has not behaved like a gentleman. She has taken an unfair advantage. I stood at the window for an hour with the hoe in my hand, like a sentry whose post has been washed away, and I fear I said some things that would not do for the church-paper.

Still, I am not wholly cast down. A garden is a great teacher of patience, and I have a good deal of it, provided it is not required of me before breakfast. The weather-man promises a clear day on Saturday; and if it holds, I shall be out there at dawn, up to my ankles in something, setting out plants and defying all prophecy.

If you should happen to be passing, bring a spade, and possibly a boat.

Yours in mud and hope,

[name]
